summary: Defines terminology and requirements for sending a location URI that points to a person's location, instead of putting the location itself in a message. It is requirements work for Internet signaling and messaging. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Instead of writing your address on a note, you hand over a card that says look it up here.

questions: location by reference vs location by value
how should a location uri be constructed
subtitle: What a protocol must do so that a location can be shared as a link instead of as raw coordinates.

tldr.problem: Sending a location directly in every message can be inefficient or undesirable, for example when a device is short on power or the operator does not want location widely available.
tldr.mechanism: Location-by-Reference hands out a location URI that points to the location. The RFC lists requirements for a configuration protocol that creates the URI and a dereference protocol that resolves it.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol. It sets the rules (random, unguessable URIs, expiry, cancellation, authentication) that later protocols are meant to meet.

today: RFC 5808 is an Informational RFC (May 2010) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It lists requirements rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Why Share a Reference Instead of a Location
sections.content:
Location can be used in two ways. With Location-by-Value (LbyV), the location object itself, such as a PIDF-LO, travels in the message. With Location-by-Reference (LbyR), a location URI stands in for the location. This document covers only the LbyR side and leaves LbyV out of scope.

The RFC gives reasons for LbyR. In some mobile networks it is not efficient for the end host to keep asking the Location Information Server (LIS) for fresh location, especially when power is limited. The host may want to delegate the job to a third party such as a presence server. And a network operator may not want location widely available.

A location URI is made of a URI scheme, a domain and a randomized component. It refers to the current location of the Target, but the value it yields may stay the same for a while, for instance because of cached location or policy.
sections.eli5: Telling everyone exactly where you are every minute is tiring and not always wise. A look-it-up card lets people ask only when they need to.

sections.title: The Players and the Life Cycle
sections.content:
The RFC reuses the RFC 3693 vocabulary: the Target (the device or person being located), the Location Server (LS), the Location Recipient (LR), the Rule Maker (RM) and the Location Object (LO). It treats a Location Server and a LIS interchangeably.

A location URI is a temporary identifier that goes through five uses: creation, distribution, conveyance, dereference and termination. Creation, distribution and termination belong to a Location Configuration Protocol. Dereference belongs to a Location Dereference Protocol. Conveyance (for example passing the URI along in SIP signaling) is out of scope here.

In the model of Figure 1, the Target gets a location URI from the LIS over a configuration protocol, gives it to the Location Recipient, and the recipient dereferences it at the LS. The LS controls access using the policy set by the Rule Maker. There is no requirement to use the same protocol for configuration and dereference. The Target can also be its own Location Recipient.
sections.eli5: One helper writes the look-it-up card, you pass the card to a friend, and the friend shows it to the helper to learn where you are. The helper checks your rules first.

sections.title: How Location URIs Are Used, Expired and Authorized
sections.content:
As an example, a Target can get a location URI in the form of a SIP subscription URI. It then subscribes to the URI and is notified of its current location, for instance when it crosses an expressed geospatial boundary. An HTTP or HTTPS URI, by contrast, is simply resolved to location information.

Location URIs may have an expiry. The RFC gives several reasons: the LIS can keep track of the URIs it handed out, can tell whether a URI is still valid, can do garbage collection, and a recipient cannot (in some cases) track a host permanently. Expiry also limits the damage if a URI leaks by accident.

The authorization model shapes how a URI looks. Under the access control model, the URI MUST NOT include location information and may be widely published, because the server decides who may dereference it. Under the possession model, the URI itself is the secret, shared between the LIS/LS, the Target and the authorized recipients, so it needs enough randomness to be hard to guess. By default a URI MUST NOT reveal anything about the Target other than location.
sections.eli5: A card can stop working after a while. Some cards only work if the helper recognises you, and some work for anyone holding the secret card, so you keep those hidden.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The configuration protocol requirements are C1 to C9. The main ones: it MUST support a location reference in URI form (C1); a limited lifetime MUST be indicated (C2); it MUST support cancelling a specific URI (C3); URIs MUST by default be random and unique so that they contain no location-specific parts (C4) and no information identifying the Target, such as phone extensions, badge numbers or names (C5); there SHOULD be a way to choose one-time or repeated resolution (C6); and the Rule Maker MUST be able to control what is disclosed (C7). A URI with 128 bits of randomness is RECOMMENDED (C8). Where a user supplies their own policy, a protocol MAY allow other URI conventions, such as embedded location (C9).

The dereference protocol requirements are D1 to D5. It MUST support URIs (D1), MUST include mechanisms to authenticate both client and server (D2), and MUST return a well-formed PIDF-LO so that privacy rules can be followed (D3). The same URI MUST be resolvable more than once, depending on server configuration, which can also limit the attempts (D4). Messages between recipient and server MUST be protected for confidentiality, for example by using an HTTPS URI (D5).

The RFC 2119 words apply to the design of the protocols, not to an implementation or application.
sections.eli5: The rules say the card must be hard to guess, must not have your name on it, can expire or be torn up, and the helper and the friend must check who the other is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Random components stop an adversary from getting location without first obtaining a URI. In the possession model, though, a publicly available URI gives no protection: anyone can dereference it. Where that is a concern, the authorization model has to be chosen, and its policies written so that only trustworthy parties get access.

Any location URI names the server that hosts the location, and knowing that server could reveal something about the Target's location. This can be eased somewhat by adding a layer of indirection, such as a remote presence server.

The RFC also notes a covert channel: if user A subscribes to the location of user B, an outside observer of each notification can tell that B has moved. One mitigation is periodic notification, so B appears to have moved even when static.
sections.eli5: If you leave the secret card on a bench, anyone can use it. Even the helper's address can hint where you are, so sometimes you use a middle helper.

messages.label: Location Configuration Protocol
messages.note: The Target acquires a location URI (1).

messages.label: Location Conveyance
messages.note: The Target passes on the URI; this interface is out of scope (2).

messages.label: Location Dereference Protocol
messages.note: The recipient resolves the URI to location information (3).
